title: How to Buy a Tokunbo Car in Nigeria Without Getting Scammed
excerpt: A practical, step-by-step guide to buying a foreign-used (Tokunbo) car in Nigeria safely - from verifying the VIN to spotting rolled-back odometers and avoiding fake dealers.
content:
Why Tokunbo cars are still the smart buy in Nigeria

For most Nigerian buyers, a Tokunbo (foreign-used) car hits the sweet spot between price and quality. These vehicles are imported from the United States, Canada or Europe, where roads are better and maintenance culture is stronger, so a well-chosen Tokunbo car often outlasts a locally-used equivalent at a similar price. But the same demand that makes Tokunbo cars popular also attracts dishonest sellers. This guide walks you through buying one without getting burned.

1. Always verify the VIN before you pay a kobo

The Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) is a 17-character code stamped on the dashboard, the driver-side door jamb, and the engine bay. It is the car's fingerprint. Before committing, run the VIN through a history service to confirm the year, make, model, accident history, title status and whether the odometer reading is consistent. At Korrect Cars, every listing shows a verifiable VIN precisely because we want buyers to check for themselves.

2. Watch out for rolled-back odometers

Odometer fraud - winding back the mileage to make a car look less used - is common. Cross-check the displayed mileage against the VIN history report, look at wear on the pedals, steering wheel and driver's seat, and be suspicious if a 10-year-old car shows unusually low kilometres with a heavily worn interior.

3. Inspect the car (or pay someone who can)

Never buy based on photos alone. Either inspect the car in person or pay for an independent pre-purchase inspection. Check the engine for leaks, listen for knocks on a cold start, test the air-conditioning, scan for dashboard warning lights, and confirm the transmission shifts smoothly. A proper inspection costs a fraction of what a bad engine will cost you later.

4. Confirm the papers are complete and genuine

Ask for the Bill of Lading, customs clearance documents and any US/Canada title. Incomplete or "we will sort the papers later" situations are a major red flag. Clean documentation protects you during registration and future resale.

5. Buy from a dealer with a reputation to protect

The safest route is a dealer who publishes real photos, transparent Naira prices, verifiable VINs and honest condition disclosures - and who is reachable after the sale. That accountability is the whole point of buying from an established online dealership rather than an anonymous roadside seller.

Final word

A Tokunbo car can serve you faithfully for years if you do your homework: verify the VIN, confirm the mileage, inspect thoroughly, demand complete papers, and buy from someone accountable. Browse verified Tokunbo cars with real photos and transparent pricing on the Korrect Cars inventory.

Common tokunbo scams and how they work

  • "Clean" cars that were salvage abroad: a car written off after an accident or flood in the US, repaired cheaply and sold as accident-free. A VIN history report and auction photos usually reveal this.
  • Swapped or cloned VINs: a stolen car given the identity of another vehicle. Check that the VIN is identical in every location and on the papers.
  • Fake customs papers: documents that look official but were never issued. Verify them and make sure the details match the car.
  • "Pay to reserve" fraud: sellers who ask for money before you have seen the car, then disappear.
  • Bait-and-switch: beautiful photos online, but a different, worse car when you arrive.

A step-by-step safe buying process

  1. Shortlist cars from reputable sellers with real addresses and honest descriptions.
  2. Get the VIN before you visit, and run a history report.
  3. Inspect in daylight with a trusted mechanic, including a diagnostic scan.
  4. Test drive for at least 20–30 minutes on different road surfaces.
  5. Verify the papers: customs documents, proof of ownership and vehicle licence, all matching the VIN.
  6. Agree the price in writing, including what is included (spare key, tools, tyres).
  7. Pay into a business account, never cash in a car park, and get a receipt listing the VIN.
  8. Collect all documents and keys, and start your change of ownership promptly.

Documents checklist

  • Customs papers showing the duty was paid for this exact VIN.
  • Proof of ownership / purchase receipt from the seller.
  • Vehicle licence and other current papers if the car is already registered.
  • Any service records and the owner's manual.
  • All keys and remotes. A missing smart key can be expensive to replace.

Signs of an honest seller

Honest sellers welcome questions. They share the VIN without hesitation, let you bring your own mechanic, point out the car's flaws, and give you time to decide. Pressure tactics like "another buyer is paying today" or refusing an inspection are your signal to walk away.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell if a tokunbo car was flooded?
Look for rust under the seats, water lines in the boot, a damp smell and electrical faults, and check the VIN history for flood records.

Is it safe to buy tokunbo cars online?
Yes, from a reputable dealer who lets you inspect the car and verify its papers before you pay.

title: Tokunbo vs Nigerian-Used vs Brand New: Which Should You Buy?
excerpt: Confused between Tokunbo, Nigerian-used and brand-new cars? We break down the real costs, risks and benefits of each so you can pick the right one for your budget.
content:
Three ways to buy a car in Nigeria

When shopping for a car in Nigeria, you generally choose between three options: a Tokunbo (foreign-used) car, a Nigerian-used car, or a brand-new car from a franchise. Each has a place depending on your budget and priorities. Here is an honest comparison.

Tokunbo (foreign-used)

Pros: Generally better maintained than locally-used cars, imported from markets with stronger maintenance culture, wide selection, and strong resale value. Prices sit comfortably below brand-new.

Cons: Condition varies, so verification matters. You need to confirm the VIN, mileage and accident history. Clearing and customs duty are already priced in when you buy from a dealer, but always confirm.

Best for: Buyers who want near-new quality at a realistic price and are willing to verify before buying.

Nigerian-used

Pros: Cheapest option upfront, already registered, and you can often meet the previous owner.

Cons: Harder-driven on Nigerian roads, more likely to have hidden mechanical issues, and mileage claims can be unreliable. The savings can evaporate quickly if the car needs major repairs.

Best for: Tight budgets, short-term needs, or buyers with a trusted mechanic who can inspect thoroughly.

Brand new

Pros: Zero history to worry about, full manufacturer warranty, latest safety and technology, and complete peace of mind.

Cons: The most expensive option by far, and it depreciates fastest in the first two to three years. Financing costs are higher because the principal is larger.

Best for: Buyers with the budget who value warranty and want the newest features.

The bottom line

For most Nigerians, a well-verified Tokunbo car offers the best balance of quality, price and resale value. A Nigerian-used car makes sense on a very tight budget if you inspect carefully, while brand-new suits those who prioritise warranty and can absorb faster depreciation. Whichever you choose, verification and honest pricing matter most. See our verified Tokunbo stock on the Korrect Cars inventory page.

Side-by-side comparison

  • Price: brand new is the most expensive; tokunbo sits in the middle; Nigerian-used is usually the cheapest.
  • Condition: brand new is perfect; tokunbo is often well kept because many were used on smooth roads abroad; Nigerian-used varies widely depending on how it was driven and maintained here.
  • History: brand new has none; tokunbo history can often be checked with a VIN report if it came from North America; Nigerian-used history is harder to verify.
  • Warranty: brand new comes with a manufacturer warranty from an authorised dealer; used cars usually don't.
  • Resale value: brand new loses value fastest in the first years; well-kept tokunbo cars of popular models tend to hold value well.

Who each option suits best

Brand new suits buyers who want complete peace of mind, a warranty and the latest features, and who can afford the higher price and early depreciation. It is also popular with companies buying fleet vehicles.

Tokunbo suits most private buyers who want a good-quality car at a reasonable price. You get more car for your money than buying new, as long as you verify the history and condition.

Nigerian-used suits buyers on a tighter budget, or those who find a car with a known history, for example from a friend or colleague who has maintained it well. The key risk is hidden wear from local road conditions.

Questions to ask any seller

  • Can I see the VIN, and does it match the papers?
  • Do you have service records?
  • Has the car ever been in an accident or flood?
  • For tokunbo: when did it arrive in Nigeria, and can I see the customs papers?
  • For Nigerian-used: how many owners has it had in Nigeria, and why are you selling?
  • Can my mechanic inspect it before I pay?

How to protect yourself whichever you choose

Whatever type of car you buy, the same rules keep you safe: verify the VIN, inspect the car in daylight, take a proper test drive, check that the papers are genuine and complete, and pay into a verifiable business account. Buying from a reputable dealer adds another layer of protection, because the dealer's reputation depends on selling honest cars.

A quick example

Imagine you have a budget for a family sedan. A brand-new car at that price might be a small entry-level model with basic features. The same money could buy a tokunbo Toyota Camry or Honda Accord a few years old, with more space, more features and a strong resale value. Alternatively, a Nigerian-used version of the same car might cost less again, leaving money for servicing and new tyres. None of these choices is wrong. The best one depends on how much risk you are comfortable with, how long you plan to keep the car, and how carefully you check its condition before you buy. Whichever route you take, budget for an inspection and a first service as part of the purchase.

Frequently asked questions

Is tokunbo better than Nigerian-used?
Often, because the car has usually been driven on better roads, but condition and history matter more than the label.

Do brand-new cars hold their value?
They lose value fastest in the first few years, which is why many Nigerian buyers prefer tokunbo.

title: How Korrect Cars Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) Works: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Own your dream car today and pay over time. Here's exactly how Korrect Cars' Buy-Now-Pay-Later financing works, who qualifies, and how to structure a plan that fits your budget.
content:
What is Buy-Now-Pay-Later for cars?

Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) lets you drive your car home after an initial down payment and pay the balance over an agreed schedule - daily, weekly or monthly. It is designed for hard-working Nigerians who have steady income but do not want to drain their savings in one payment. At Korrect Cars, BNPL is a core part of how we help people own quality vehicles.

How the process works, step by step

1. Choose your car. Browse the inventory and pick a verified vehicle within your reach.

2. Agree the down payment. You make an initial payment that fits your budget. A larger down payment means smaller instalments and lower total cost.

3. Sign the BNPL agreement. The contract clearly states the down payment, instalment amount, tenure, and what happens if payments are missed. Read it fully before signing.

4. Drive home. Once the agreement is in place, the car is delivered to you.

5. Pay on schedule. You settle the balance on the agreed daily, weekly or monthly plan until the car is fully yours.

Who qualifies?

Approval depends on verifiable income and a straightforward background check. Salary earners, business owners and professionals with consistent cash flow are typically good candidates. The paperwork is simple and approvals are fast.

Tips for a smart BNPL plan

  • Put down as much as you comfortably can. It lowers your instalments and total interest.
  • Match instalments to your pay cycle. If you are paid monthly, a monthly plan is easiest to manage.
  • Keep an emergency buffer. Don't stretch so far that one bad month causes a default.
  • Understand the default terms. Know exactly what happens if you miss a payment before you sign.

Why BNPL beats waiting

Car prices rarely fall, and needing reliable transport for work or family often cannot wait. BNPL lets you start using the car - and the income or convenience it enables - while you pay it off. Speak to the Korrect Cars team to structure a plan around your budget, or explore financing-friendly vehicles on our inventory.

Documents you may be asked for

Exact requirements depend on the financing partner, but applicants are commonly asked for:

  • A valid government-issued ID (NIN slip, international passport, driver's licence or voter's card).
  • Your BVN for identity and credit checks.
  • Recent bank statements, usually covering the last few months, to show regular income.
  • Proof of address, such as a recent utility bill.
  • For employees: an employment letter or recent payslips. For business owners: business registration documents and business account statements.

Having these ready speeds up approval considerably.

Understanding the total cost

A payment plan makes a car affordable today, but it is important to understand what you will pay in total. Before you sign, ask for a clear breakdown of:

  • The down payment required.
  • The monthly (or weekly) instalment and how many payments there are.
  • The interest rate or financing charge, and whether it is fixed.
  • Any fees for processing, insurance, tracking devices or documentation.
  • What happens if you pay early: are there savings or penalties?
  • What happens if you miss a payment.

Multiply the instalment by the number of payments and add the down payment and fees. That total is the true price of the car on the plan.

How to choose the right plan for your budget

A good rule of thumb is to keep your car payment at a level you can comfortably meet even in a slow month, leaving room for fuel, maintenance and insurance. A larger down payment reduces your monthly instalment and the total financing cost. A shorter plan usually costs less overall but has higher instalments. Choose what you can sustain, not the most expensive car you can be approved for.

BNPL vs saving up vs a bank loan

Saving the full amount avoids financing costs, but it can take years while car prices keep rising. A traditional bank car loan may offer competitive rates but often requires more paperwork and a longer approval process. A dealer-arranged payment plan sits in between: it is designed around the car purchase, so approval and delivery are usually quicker. Compare the total cost of each option, not just the monthly figure, and choose the one that fits your income and timeline.

Common questions

Who owns the car while I'm paying?
This depends on the agreement. In many plans the financing partner keeps an interest in the car until it is fully paid, after which ownership documents are transferred to you. Read the agreement carefully.

Is insurance required?
Most financing plans require comprehensive insurance for the duration of the plan, because the car is the security for the loan.

Can I pay off early?
Often yes. Ask whether early payment reduces the total cost.

What if my income changes?
Speak to the financing partner early. It is always easier to agree a solution before payments are missed.

Talk to us before you apply

If you are unsure which car or plan suits your budget, contact Korrect Cars. We will explain the options available through our financing partner and help you choose a car you can comfortably afford.

title: Understanding Customs Duty and Clearing Costs on Imported Cars in Nigeria
excerpt: Import duty, clearing fees, terminal charges and more - here's a plain-English breakdown of what it really costs to clear a car in Nigeria and why dealer prices already include it.
content:
Why clearing costs matter to every car buyer

When you buy an imported car in Nigeria, part of what you pay covers the cost of getting that car legally through the ports. Understanding these customs and clearing costs helps you judge whether a price is fair and why some "cheap" cars end up costing more later.

The main components of clearing a car

Import duty: The Nigeria Customs Service charges duty based on the vehicle's category and assessed value. Larger, higher-value vehicles attract more.

Levy: Certain vehicles attract an additional levy on top of the base duty, depending on prevailing policy.

Terminal and shipping-line charges: The terminal operators and shipping lines charge handling, storage and documentation fees.

Clearing agent fees: A licensed agent handles the paperwork and physical clearing, and charges for the service.

Miscellaneous: Examination, transport from the port, and other small charges add up.

Why a dealer price is often the safer deal

When you buy an already-cleared car from a reputable dealer, the duty and clearing costs are baked into the price and the car is ready to register. Buying an "uncleared" car directly can look cheaper on paper, but you then carry the risk of fluctuating duty, demurrage if clearing is delayed, and agent problems. For most buyers, a transparently-priced, already-cleared vehicle removes stress and hidden cost.

Questions to ask before you buy

  • Is the car fully cleared with complete documentation?
  • Can I see the Bill of Lading and customs papers?
  • Is the price all-in, or are there charges to come?

The takeaway

Clearing a car in Nigeria involves duty, levies, terminal charges and agent fees that can add significantly to the landed cost. Buying an already-cleared, transparently-priced vehicle from an accountable dealer protects you from surprises. Every car on the Korrect Cars inventory is priced in clear Naira with documentation available on request.

The main charges explained in plain language

Customs charges on imported vehicles in Nigeria are calculated by the Nigeria Customs Service and can change with government policy, so always confirm current rates before you import. In general, the cost of bringing a car into the country is made up of several parts:

  • Import duty: a percentage of the car's assessed customs value.
  • Levy and surcharges: additional charges set by government policy on top of the duty.
  • VAT: value added tax applied to the total.
  • Port and terminal charges: fees paid to the shipping terminal for handling and storage. Storage charges grow every day the car stays at the port.
  • Shipping line charges: fees from the shipping company for releasing the vehicle.
  • Clearing agent fees: what you pay a licensed agent to handle documents and processes on your behalf.
  • Transport from the port: moving the car from Lagos ports to your location.

How the customs value is worked out

Duty is not based on what you say you paid for the car. Customs assesses a value using the car's make, model, year and condition, often with reference to standard price guides. That is why two cars bought for similar prices at auction can attract different duties, and why older cars are not always much cheaper to clear than you might expect.

Common mistakes that raise costs

  • Delays at the port: every extra day can add storage and demurrage charges.
  • Incomplete documents: missing or inconsistent paperwork leads to delays and penalties.
  • Using unlicensed agents: always work with a licensed customs agent and get receipts for official payments.
  • Under-declaring value: this can lead to penalties and seizure. It is never worth the risk.
  • Ignoring the car's condition: a cheap damaged car still attracts full charges, and repairs come on top.

Buying already-cleared vs importing yourself

Importing yourself can make sense if you have experience, a trusted agent and time to manage the process. For most buyers, buying a car that is already cleared from a reputable dealer is simpler: the price is known upfront, the customs papers can be verified, and you avoid port delays and surprise charges. Always ask to see the customs documents and confirm that the VIN on them matches the car.

An example of how the costs add up

Consider two buyers who each find a car abroad for a similar price. The first uses an experienced, licensed agent, has complete documents ready and clears the car within days. The second has a missing document, waits for weeks, and pays daily storage charges while the problem is fixed. Even though both paid the same duty, the second buyer's total cost ends up much higher. Time at the port is money, which is why preparation and a reliable agent matter as much as the duty itself.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I check current customs duty rates?
From the Nigeria Customs Service and its official channels, or through a licensed clearing agent.

How do I know a car was properly cleared?
Ask for the customs papers, check that the VIN matches, and verify them through official channels if in doubt.

title: Best Family SUVs to Buy in Lagos in 2026
excerpt: Space, comfort, reliability and resale value - here are the family SUVs that make the most sense for Lagos roads and Nigerian families in 2026.
content:
What makes a great family SUV in Nigeria

For a Nigerian family, the right SUV needs ground clearance for rough roads and flooded streets, strong air-conditioning for the heat, room for children and luggage, good reliability, and healthy resale value. Here are the SUVs that consistently deliver in Lagos.

Toyota Highlander

The Highlander is a Lagos favourite for good reason: three rows of seating, bulletproof Toyota reliability, comfortable ride, and excellent resale. It swallows a full family plus luggage and handles poor roads with ease. Parts are everywhere and mechanics know it inside out.

Lexus RX 350

If you want Toyota reliability wrapped in genuine luxury, the RX 350 is hard to beat. Quiet cabin, plush ride, premium interior, and a strong resale reputation. It is the SUV that says you have arrived without the running-cost headaches of some European rivals.

Mercedes-Benz GLE / ML 350

For buyers who want a premium badge and a commanding drive, the GLE (and its predecessor, the ML) offer German build quality, a high-tech cabin and strong road presence. Choose a well-verified example and budget a little more for maintenance, and you get a genuinely upscale family SUV.

Toyota RAV4

Smaller and more fuel-efficient than the Highlander, the RAV4 is ideal for families who want SUV practicality without a large thirst. Reliable, easy to park in tight Lagos spots, and cheap to run.

How to choose

  • Big family, long trips: Highlander or a three-row option.
  • Luxury on a sensible budget: Lexus RX 350.
  • Premium badge and tech: Mercedes-Benz GLE or ML 350.
  • Fuel economy and city ease: Toyota RAV4.

Final thought

The best family SUV is the one that matches your budget, seating needs and running-cost comfort. Whichever you lean towards, verify the VIN and condition before buying. Explore family-ready SUVs on the Korrect Cars inventory.

Comparing the options at a glance

  • Most seats: Toyota Highlander, with three rows on most versions, ideal for larger families and school runs.
  • Most comfort for the money: Lexus RX 350, quiet and smooth with a reputation for reliability.
  • Most prestige and technology: Mercedes-Benz GLE / ML 350, with strong safety features and road presence.
  • Lowest running costs: Toyota RAV4, a compact SUV with four-cylinder or hybrid options that are cheaper in traffic.

Safety features worth paying for

For a family car, safety comes first. When comparing SUVs, look for:

  • Plenty of airbags, including side and curtain airbags.
  • Stability control and anti-lock brakes (standard on most modern SUVs).
  • A reverse camera and parking sensors, very useful in crowded Lagos car parks.
  • Blind-spot monitoring and lane assistance on newer models.
  • ISOFIX anchor points to fit children's car seats securely.
  • Good crash-test results; check the model's rating with organisations such as the US IIHS or Euro NCAP.

Practical things families forget to check

  • Boot space with all seats in use: some seven-seaters have very little room for bags when the third row is up.
  • Rear air-conditioning: in Nigerian heat, rear vents or a separate rear AC make a big difference for children.
  • Ease of getting in and out: try the third row yourself; consider grandparents and young children.
  • Ground clearance: important for flooded streets and rough estate roads.
  • Fuel economy in traffic: a big V6 or V8 can be costly on daily school runs.

Buying used: what matters most

Most families buy their SUV tokunbo or Nigerian-used. Whatever model you choose, check the VIN history, have the car professionally inspected, and look for proof of regular servicing. A well-maintained Highlander or RX 350 can serve a family for many years; a neglected one can become a constant source of expense.

New vs older family SUVs

A newer SUV brings better safety technology, more efficient engines and modern features like Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. An older model costs less upfront and may be simpler to repair, but it can lack features such as blind-spot monitoring and may need more maintenance. For many families, a model that is a few years old offers the best balance: modern safety features at a much lower price than new.

Test-drive tips for families

Bring the family along if you can. Fit your child seats, check that everyone is comfortable, and load the boot with the kind of bags you carry on a typical trip. Drive over speed bumps and a rough road to judge the ride quality, and test the rear air-conditioning on a hot afternoon. A car that looks perfect in a showroom can feel very different on the school run.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best seven-seater SUV for a Nigerian family?
The Toyota Highlander is the most popular choice thanks to its space, reliability and easy parts.

Is a hybrid SUV a good family car?
Yes, if you drive mostly in traffic and have access to a mechanic who understands hybrids.

title: 2016 Mercedes-Benz GLE 350 Buyer's Guide: What to Know Before You Buy
excerpt: Thinking of buying a 2016 Mercedes-Benz GLE 350? Here's what to check, what it's like to own in Nigeria, and how to spot a good example.
content:
The GLE 350: Mercedes' luxury SUV sweet spot

The 2016 Mercedes-Benz GLE 350 is the mid-size luxury SUV that many Nigerian buyers aspire to - refined, comfortable, and carrying that unmistakable three-pointed-star prestige. It replaced the ML-Class and brought sharper styling and a more modern cabin. Here is what to know before buying one.

What you get

Under the bonnet sits a smooth 3.5-litre V6 producing around 302 horsepower, paired with a 7-speed automatic and, on 4MATIC versions, permanent all-wheel drive. Inside you get a high-quality cabin with wood and aluminium trim, an 8-inch display, dual-zone climate, power-heated seats and a long list of driver-assistance features. Many examples come with a panoramic sunroof and 360-degree camera.

What to check before buying

  • Air suspension (if fitted): Confirm the ride height settles correctly and there are no leaks.
  • Electronics: Test the COMAND system, cameras, climate control and all seat functions.
  • Service history: A well-maintained GLE is a joy; a neglected one can be costly. Look for evidence of regular servicing.
  • Certified Pre-Owned origin: Some units were sold as Mercedes-Benz Certified Pre-Owned, meaning they were inspected and reconditioned before export - a strong plus.

Owning one in Nigeria

The GLE handles Nigerian roads well thanks to good ground clearance and a compliant ride. Running costs are higher than a Toyota, but parts and specialist mechanics are available in Lagos. Budget for premium fuel and periodic servicing, and it will reward you with a genuinely upscale driving experience.

Is it worth it?

If you want a luxury SUV with presence, comfort and technology at a fraction of its new price, a well-verified 2016 GLE 350 is an excellent buy. Just insist on a clean VIN, complete electronics and evidence of care. See current GLE listings on the Korrect Cars inventory.

GLE 350 vs ML 350: what changed

From the 2016 model year, Mercedes renamed the M-Class (ML) as the GLE. The 2016 GLE 350 is essentially an updated version of the last ML 350, with a refreshed design, updated interior and a newer 9-speed automatic gearbox in many markets. In Nigeria both names are common, and parts are often shared, which helps keep repairs manageable. If you are comparing a late ML 350 with an early GLE 350, focus on condition and history rather than the badge.

Running costs to plan for

  • Fuel: the V6 is smooth and capable, but expect higher consumption than a four-cylinder SUV, especially in traffic.
  • Servicing: use the correct Mercedes-approved oil and have the car serviced by a workshop with Mercedes diagnostic equipment.
  • Tyres and brakes: larger wheels and a heavier vehicle mean higher costs than a mid-size Japanese SUV.
  • Electronics: modern Mercedes models are packed with sensors and modules; an electrical fault diagnosed by guesswork can become expensive.

Inspection checklist specific to the GLE 350

  • Air suspension (if fitted): the car should sit level after standing and the suspension should raise and lower without warning messages.
  • Gearbox: shifts should be smooth; hesitation or harsh changes need investigating.
  • Oil leaks: look around the engine and underneath, particularly on high-mileage cars.
  • Warning messages: scroll through the instrument cluster for stored alerts, and run a diagnostic scan.
  • 4MATIC: on all-wheel-drive versions, listen for clunks or whining on tight turns.
  • Paperwork: confirm the VIN matches the papers and check the history report for accident or flood records.

Certified pre-owned: what it should mean

When a car is described as "certified pre-owned", ask exactly what was checked and by whom, and request the inspection report. A genuine certification process should include a multi-point inspection, a diagnostic scan, replacement of worn items and a clear account of the car's history. Certification adds confidence, but you are still entitled to have your own mechanic look at the car.

Alternatives worth comparing

If you are shopping for a GLE 350, it is worth also looking at the Lexus RX 350 (lower running costs, very reliable), the BMW X5 (sportier to drive) and the Toyota Highlander (more practical for big families). The GLE stands out for its blend of comfort, safety technology and road presence.

Who the GLE 350 suits best

The GLE 350 is ideal for buyers who want a comfortable, safe and prestigious SUV for daily driving and family trips, and who are prepared to maintain it properly. It suits professionals who drive long distances on highways, families who value safety technology, and anyone who wants Mercedes luxury without the much higher costs of AMG models. If your priority is the lowest possible running cost, a Lexus RX 350 or Toyota Highlander may be the more practical choice.

Frequently asked questions

Is the GLE 350 reliable?
A well-maintained GLE 350 is a dependable SUV. Service history and correct maintenance matter more than anything.

Can I use regular fuel?
Follow the fuel recommendation in the owner's manual and buy from reputable stations.

title: 2013 Lexus RX 350 Review: Why It's One of the Smartest Buys in Nigeria
excerpt: Reliable, luxurious and holding its value for over a decade - here's why the 2013 Lexus RX 350 remains one of the smartest used-car buys in Nigeria.
content:
The RX 350: luxury that refuses to break down

Few cars have earned Nigerian trust like the Lexus RX 350. The 2013 model, part of the facelifted third generation, blends Toyota's legendary reliability with genuine luxury - and it holds its value better than almost anything in its class. Here is why it remains such a smart buy.

What makes it special

The RX 350 uses a proven 3.5-litre V6 (the same family found in reliable Toyota models) making around 275 horsepower through a smooth 6-speed automatic. The cabin is quiet, plush and beautifully built, with soft leather, wood trim and a comfortable ride that soaks up Lagos potholes. It is the definition of stress-free luxury motoring.

Reliability you can count on

This is the RX 350's headline feature. The drivetrain is famously durable, parts are widely available, and almost every competent mechanic in Nigeria knows the car. That combination keeps running costs low and resale value high - an RX 350 bought today will still command strong money years from now.

What to check

  • Service history and mileage consistency: Verify the VIN and cross-check the odometer.
  • Suspension and brakes: Normal wear items; budget for them if the car has covered high mileage.
  • Infotainment and camera: Confirm everything works.
  • Interior wear: A well-kept cabin signals a cared-for car.

Who should buy one

The RX 350 suits professionals and families who want understated luxury, low drama and excellent resale. It is comfortable, safe, spacious enough for a family, and cheap to keep on the road relative to European rivals.

The verdict

A clean, well-verified 2013 Lexus RX 350 is one of the safest luxury buys in the Nigerian market. It delivers comfort and prestige without the maintenance anxiety, and it protects your money at resale time. Browse available Lexus models on the Korrect Cars inventory.

Why the RX 350 suits Nigerian roads

The RX 350 combines a comfortable, quiet ride with enough ground clearance for speed bumps and broken roads. Its suspension is tuned for comfort, so it absorbs potholes better than many sportier SUVs. The 3.5-litre V6 has been used across many Toyota and Lexus models, which means mechanics in Nigeria know it well and parts are easier to find than for most luxury brands.

Running costs

Compared with German luxury SUVs, the RX 350 is generally cheaper to keep on the road. Routine items like oil changes, filters, brake pads and spark plugs are straightforward, and many parts are shared with Toyota models such as the Highlander. Fuel use is higher than a four-cylinder SUV, so expect bigger bills in heavy traffic. Comprehensive insurance is a good idea for a car of this value.

Common issues to look out for

The RX 350 has a strong reputation, but no car is perfect. When inspecting one, pay particular attention to:

  • Transmission behaviour: shifts should be smooth with no slipping, flaring or harsh jerks.
  • Oil leaks around the engine, particularly on older, high-mileage cars.
  • Dashboard and infotainment: make sure the screen, navigation, reverse camera and controls all work.
  • Suspension noises over bumps, which may mean worn bushings or shock absorbers.
  • Service history: regular oil changes are the best predictor of a long engine life.

RX 350 vs the competition

Against the Mercedes GLE or BMW X5, the RX 350 trades a little driving excitement for comfort, reliability and lower running costs. Against the Toyota Highlander, it offers a more upmarket cabin and a quieter ride, but only two rows of seats (except for the longer RX L versions), so families who need seven seats may prefer the Highlander.

Is a 2013 RX 350 still a good buy?

For many buyers, yes. A well-kept 2013 RX 350 offers luxury, comfort and dependability at a fraction of the price of a new SUV. The key words are "well-kept": insist on a VIN check, a professional inspection and a proper test drive, and favour cars with service records.

Choosing the right RX 350 year

Each RX generation brought improvements. Later models generally have more safety technology, updated infotainment and refined styling, while earlier models cost less and are simpler. When comparing years, look at the specific car rather than the model year alone: a carefully maintained older RX with full service records is often a better buy than a newer one with an unclear history. Check the trim level too, as features like navigation, premium audio and ventilated seats vary between versions.

If you plan to keep the car for many years, favour lower mileage and documented maintenance. If you plan to sell in a year or two, a popular colour and trim will make resale easier.

Frequently asked questions

Is the RX 350 expensive to maintain?
Less than most luxury SUVs, because it shares many parts with Toyota models.

Does it have seven seats?
The standard RX 350 seats five. The longer RX 350L, available in later years, adds a third row.

title: Toyota Camry vs Toyota Avalon: Which Sedan Is Right for You?
excerpt: Both are reliable Toyota sedans, but they serve different buyers. Here's a clear comparison of the Camry and Avalon to help you choose.
content:
Two Toyota sedans, two different buyers

The Toyota Camry and Toyota Avalon are both dependable, resale-friendly sedans that dominate Nigerian roads. They share Toyota's reliability DNA but target slightly different needs. Here is how to choose between them.

Toyota Camry: the sensible all-rounder

The Camry is the practical choice - right-sized for city and highway, fuel-efficient, comfortable, and cheaper to buy and run than the Avalon. It offers a roomy cabin, a smooth ride, and the strongest resale value in its class. For most buyers who want a reliable daily sedan that just works, the Camry is the default answer.

Best for: Everyday commuting, ride-hailing, first-time buyers, and anyone prioritising fuel economy and low running costs.

Toyota Avalon: the near-luxury flagship

The Avalon is larger, plusher and quieter - Toyota's full-size flagship sedan. It offers more rear legroom, a more upscale interior, and a serene highway cruise that approaches luxury-car territory. It costs a bit more to buy and drinks slightly more fuel, but it rewards you with genuine comfort and presence.

Best for: Executives, families wanting extra space, and buyers who want near-luxury comfort without a premium badge's running costs.

Head to head

  • Price: Camry is more affordable.
  • Fuel economy: Camry edges it.
  • Comfort and space: Avalon wins.
  • Reliability and resale: Both excellent.

The bottom line

Choose the Camry if you want the most sensible, economical reliable sedan. Choose the Avalon if you want more space and near-luxury comfort and can stretch the budget slightly. Either way you get Toyota dependability. See both models on the Korrect Cars inventory.

Comfort and space

Both cars are roomy enough for five adults, but the Avalon is built to pamper. It has a longer wheelbase than the Camry, which translates into more rear legroom and a calmer ride on rough roads. Its seats are softer, its cabin is quieter at speed, and higher trims add features usually found in luxury cars, such as ventilated seats and premium audio. The Camry is comfortable too, and its tighter suspension makes it feel a little more agile in town. If you often carry passengers in the back, or you are driven rather than driving, the Avalon has a clear edge.

Running costs in Nigeria

This is where the Camry shines. It is one of the most common cars on Nigerian roads, so parts are available almost everywhere, from Ladipo to small roadside shops, and almost every mechanic knows it inside out. Most Camrys use a four-cylinder engine, which is cheaper to run in traffic. The Avalon usually comes with a V6 (except hybrid versions), which uses more fuel, and some of its trim and body parts are less common, so they can take longer to find and cost more.

Resale value

The Camry is famous for holding its value in Nigeria. Demand is constant, which makes it easy to sell when you want to upgrade. The Avalon also holds value well among buyers who know it, but the pool of buyers is smaller, so it can take longer to sell at a good price.

Which generation should you buy?

For both models, newer generations bring better safety technology, improved fuel economy and modern infotainment. Whatever year you choose, check the car's history with a VIN report, confirm that the timing and service work has been done, and test every electronic feature before you buy. A well-maintained older car is usually a better buy than a neglected newer one.

Our recommendation

  • Choose the Camry if you drive yourself, spend a lot of time in traffic, and want the lowest running costs and easiest resale.
  • Choose the Avalon if comfort and quietness matter most, you carry passengers regularly, and you are happy to pay a little more to run it.

Safety and technology

Both sedans benefit from Toyota's strong safety record, and newer model years come with Toyota Safety Sense features such as pre-collision warning, lane departure alert and adaptive cruise control. The Avalon usually offers more comfort and convenience features as standard, while the Camry lets you choose from a wide range of trims, from basic to well-equipped. Whichever you choose, check that the reverse camera, sensors and infotainment all work, as these can be costly to fix.

Test drive them back to back

If you can, drive both cars on the same day and the same roads. Pay attention to ride comfort over bumps, noise at highway speed, rear-seat space and visibility. Many buyers who expect to choose the Avalon end up preferring the Camry's lighter feel, and the reverse is also true. Your own impression matters more than any review.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Avalon a luxury car?
It is Toyota's flagship sedan and feels close to a Lexus in comfort, but it is still a Toyota in terms of running costs.

Which is better for Uber or ride-hailing?
Usually the Camry, because of its lower fuel use and cheaper parts.

title: How to Verify a Car's VIN Before Buying in Nigeria
excerpt: The VIN is your best protection against fraud. Learn where to find it, how to read it, and how to use it to confirm a car's true history before you buy.
content:
The VIN: a car's fingerprint

The Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) is a unique 17-character code that identifies every car ever built. Learning to find and verify it is the single most powerful thing you can do to avoid buying a stolen, cloned, salvaged or odometer-tampered vehicle in Nigeria.

Where to find the VIN

  • Dashboard: Visible through the windscreen on the driver's side.
  • Driver-side door jamb: On a sticker or metal plate when you open the door.
  • Engine bay: Stamped on the firewall or a component.
  • Vehicle documents: Printed on the title and customs papers.

Confirm the VIN matches in all these places. A mismatch is a serious warning sign.

How to read a VIN

Each character carries meaning. The first three identify the manufacturer and country of origin, the middle section describes the vehicle's attributes (model, engine, body), and the later characters encode the model year and a unique serial number. You don't need to memorise this - a VIN decoder or history report translates it for you.

What a VIN check reveals

  • Accident and damage history
  • Title status (clean, salvage, rebuilt)
  • Odometer readings over time - exposing rollback fraud
  • Number of previous owners
  • Whether the year and model match the seller's claim

Putting it to use

Before you pay, ask the seller for the VIN and run it through a reputable history service. Compare the report to the car in front of you - year, colour, mileage and condition should all line up. If a seller refuses to share the VIN, walk away.

Buy where the VIN is already on show

The best dealers publish the VIN openly so you can verify before you visit. Every listing on the Korrect Cars inventory includes a verifiable VIN for exactly this reason - transparency you can check for yourself.

Step by step: checking a VIN before you buy

  1. Find the VIN in at least three places: the base of the windscreen on the driver's side, the sticker or plate on the driver's door pillar, and on the papers (customs documents and proof of ownership). On many cars it is also stamped on the chassis or engine bay.
  2. Make sure they all match exactly. All 17 characters must be the same everywhere. Any difference is a serious warning sign.
  3. Look at the condition of the VIN plates. Scratches, loose rivets, glue marks or stickers that look newer than the car can indicate tampering.
  4. Decode it. Free online VIN decoders will tell you the make, model, year, engine and where the car was built. Check this against what the seller says.
  5. Run a history report. For cars imported from the United States or Canada, paid services such as Carfax and AutoCheck show title records, accident history, auction records and odometer readings. Many buyers in Nigeria use these before buying a tokunbo car.
  6. Look up auction photos. Many imported cars were sold at auctions such as Copart or IAAI, and photos of the car as it was sold are often still online. They can reveal damage that has since been repaired.

Understanding US title brands

If a history report shows a "branded" title, understand what it means before you go further:

  • Clean: no major insurance write-off recorded.
  • Salvage: the insurer declared the car a total loss, usually after an accident, flood or theft.
  • Rebuilt or reconstructed: a salvage car that was repaired and inspected.
  • Flood: the car was damaged by water. Treat these with extreme caution.

A salvage or rebuilt car is not automatically bad, but it should be priced much lower, and the quality of the repair matters enormously. Always get a professional inspection.

What a VIN check cannot tell you

A VIN report is powerful but not perfect. Accidents that were never reported to an insurer won't appear, and records stop once a car leaves its original country. That is why a VIN check should always be combined with a physical inspection and a test drive.

Where Korrect Cars stands

We believe every buyer should be able to see a car's VIN before paying anything. That is why we share the VIN of the cars we sell on request, and encourage buyers to run their own checks and bring their own mechanic. Transparency is the simplest way to build trust in the Nigerian car market, and it protects honest sellers as much as buyers.

Frequently asked questions

How many characters does a VIN have?
Modern VINs have 17 characters and never use the letters I, O or Q, to avoid confusion with numbers.

Can I check a Nigerian-used car's VIN?
Yes. Decoding works for any modern car, and if it was imported from North America, its earlier history may still be available.

The seller won't share the VIN. What should I do?
Walk away. A genuine seller has no reason to hide it.

title: Car Maintenance Tips for Nigerian Roads
excerpt: Nigerian roads are tough on cars. These practical maintenance tips will keep your vehicle reliable, safe and holding its value for longer.
content:
Why maintenance matters more in Nigeria

Potholes, flooding, heat, dust and stop-start traffic make Nigerian roads especially demanding. A little proactive car maintenance goes a long way toward keeping your vehicle reliable, safe and valuable. Here are the habits that protect your investment.

1. Change oil and filters on schedule

Heat and traffic put extra strain on your engine oil. Stick to the recommended change interval - or slightly sooner if you sit in heavy traffic daily - and always replace the oil filter with the oil. Clean oil is the cheapest insurance against expensive engine damage.

2. Check your tyres and suspension often

Potholes destroy tyres, wheels and suspension components. Inspect tyre pressure and tread regularly, rotate tyres periodically, and listen for knocks or clunks that signal worn shock absorbers, bushes or control arms. Good tyres and suspension keep you safe and comfortable.

3. Look after your cooling system

Nigerian heat and traffic make overheating a real risk. Keep the coolant topped up, watch the temperature gauge, and service the radiator and water pump as needed. An overheating engine can fail catastrophically.

4. Service the air-conditioning

In this climate, air-conditioning is not a luxury. Have the system checked, keep the cabin filter clean, and re-gas when cooling weakens. It also keeps dust out of your lungs.

5. Protect against flooding

During the rains, avoid driving through deep water - it can be sucked into the engine and cause serious damage. If you must cross water, go slowly and steadily, and never restart an engine that has stalled in flood water.

6. Keep the battery and electrics healthy

Heat shortens battery life. Check terminals for corrosion, keep them clean and tight, and replace an ageing battery before it strands you.

Maintenance is cheaper than repair

Every one of these habits costs far less than the repair it prevents - and a well-maintained car sells for more when the time comes. If you need servicing support, Korrect Cars can help with inspection and maintenance. Browse well-kept vehicles on our inventory.

A simple maintenance calendar

Every car is different, so always follow your owner's manual first. As a general guide for Nigerian conditions:

  • Every week: check tyre pressures, look for leaks under the car, and make sure all lights work.
  • Every month: check engine oil, coolant, brake fluid and windscreen washer levels; clean battery terminals if you see white or green deposits.
  • Every 5,000–10,000 km (or as your manual says): change engine oil and the oil filter; inspect brakes and tyres.
  • Every 15,000–20,000 km: replace the air filter (sooner if you drive on dusty roads) and the cabin filter.
  • Every 1–2 years: change brake fluid and coolant, and have the AC system serviced.
  • At the manufacturer's interval: replace the timing belt (if your engine has one) and spark plugs. A broken timing belt can destroy an engine.

Warning lights you should never ignore

  • Oil pressure light (red oil can): stop as soon as it is safe. Driving on can ruin the engine within minutes.
  • Temperature warning: pull over and let the engine cool. Never open a hot radiator cap.
  • Battery or charging light: your alternator may be failing; the car could stop when the battery runs flat.
  • Brake warning: check brake fluid and have the system inspected immediately.
  • Check engine light: not always urgent, but get it scanned soon. If it is flashing, reduce speed and see a mechanic right away.

Choosing a good mechanic

The right mechanic saves you money for years. Look for someone who explains what is wrong and shows you the old parts, gives you a price before starting work, uses a diagnostic scanner rather than guessing, and is recommended by people you trust. Be cautious of anyone who always finds expensive problems or insists on cash with no receipt.

Driving habits that protect your car

  • Slow down for potholes and speed bumps; hitting them hard damages suspension and tyres.
  • Avoid driving through deep floodwater. Water sucked into the engine can cause catastrophic damage.
  • Let the engine idle for a few seconds after starting, then drive gently until it warms up.
  • Don't overload the car beyond its rated capacity.
  • Buy fuel from reputable stations to reduce the risk of contaminated fuel.

Keep a simple service record

Keep every receipt and write down the date, mileage and work done each time your car is serviced. A small notebook in the glovebox or a note on your phone is enough. A clear service history helps your mechanic spot patterns, reminds you when the next job is due, and adds real value when you sell, because buyers pay more for a car with proof of care.

Frequently asked questions

Synthetic or mineral oil?
Use the grade and type in your owner's manual. Many modern engines require synthetic oil.

How do I know if my car was flooded?
See our inspection checklist for the signs, and have a mechanic check the electrics if you suspect it.

title: The Real Cost of Owning a Car in Lagos
excerpt: Beyond the purchase price, owning a car in Lagos comes with fuel, maintenance, insurance and more. Here's an honest breakdown to help you budget properly.
content:
Looking beyond the sticker price

Buying a car is only the beginning. To own one comfortably in Lagos, you need to budget for the running costs that follow. Understanding these upfront prevents nasty surprises and helps you choose a car you can actually afford to keep.

Fuel

Fuel is usually the biggest ongoing cost, and Lagos traffic makes it worse - stop-start driving burns far more than open-road cruising. A smaller, fuel-efficient engine can save you meaningfully every month. If you cover long distances daily, prioritise economy when choosing your car.

Maintenance and repairs

Routine servicing - oil, filters, brakes, tyres - is predictable and manageable. The wildcard is unexpected repairs, which is why buying a well-verified car and maintaining it proactively pays off. Japanese brands like Toyota and Lexus keep this cost low; premium European cars cost more to maintain.

Insurance

At minimum you need third-party insurance, but comprehensive cover is wise for a valuable vehicle, protecting you against theft, fire and accident. Premiums vary with the car's value and your coverage level.

Registration, licensing and papers

Vehicle registration, plate number, roadworthiness and other statutory documents are recurring costs you must keep current to drive legally and avoid fines.

Parking, tolls and miscellaneous

Depending on where you live and work, budget for parking, occasional tolls, car washes, and small consumables like wiper blades and bulbs.

How to keep total cost of ownership low

  • Choose a reliable, fuel-efficient model with cheap, available parts.
  • Buy a well-verified car to avoid inheriting someone else's problems.
  • Maintain proactively - prevention is cheaper than repair.
  • Consider resale value - cars that hold value cost less to own over time.

Budget smart, drive happy

The cheapest car to buy is not always the cheapest to own. Factor in fuel, maintenance, insurance and papers, and choose a vehicle that fits your whole budget - not just the purchase price. Explore reliable, resale-friendly cars on the Korrect Cars inventory.

A simple way to estimate your yearly cost

Before you buy, sit down with a notebook or spreadsheet and estimate what the car will really cost you each year. A simple method:

  1. Fuel: estimate how many kilometres you drive per week, multiply by 52, then work out the litres needed using the car's real-world consumption in traffic (not the brochure figure) and today's pump price.
  2. Servicing: count how many oil changes and services you will need per year and get a quote from your mechanic.
  3. Tyres, brakes and battery: spread the cost of these wear items over their expected life.
  4. Insurance and papers: add your insurance premium and the yearly renewal of your vehicle licence, road worthiness and other documents.
  5. Unexpected repairs: set aside a monthly amount for surprises. Older cars need a bigger buffer.

Add it all up and divide by 12. That monthly figure, not just the price tag, is what tells you whether a car is truly affordable.

Why the "cheapest" car is not always the cheapest

A low purchase price can hide high running costs. An older luxury car might cost the same as a newer Toyota Corolla, but its parts, tyres and fuel bills can be several times higher. Popular models like the Corolla, Camry, Honda Accord and Toyota Highlander are cheaper to own in Nigeria because parts are everywhere, almost every mechanic knows them, and they hold their resale value well. When you sell, a well-kept popular model will usually bring back more of your money.

Depreciation: the cost nobody sees

Every car loses value over time, and this is often the biggest cost of all, even though you never pay it as a bill. Luxury cars and less common models usually lose value faster. Keeping service records, avoiding accidents and keeping the car clean can protect a surprising amount of resale value.

Ways owners in Lagos cut costs

  • Find one trusted mechanic and stay with them; they learn your car and catch problems early.
  • Buy genuine or good-quality parts. Cheap fake parts often fail quickly and cost more in the end.
  • Compare insurance quotes every year instead of renewing automatically.
  • Keep all papers up to date to avoid fines and impoundment fees.
  • Consider how you will pay. A structured payment plan can make a better car affordable without draining your savings.

Plan for the unexpected

Even well-maintained cars need occasional unplanned repairs. Setting aside a small amount every month for this means a sudden repair becomes an inconvenience rather than a crisis, and you won't be tempted to delay important work.

Frequently asked questions

Is third-party insurance compulsory in Nigeria?
Yes, third-party motor insurance is a legal requirement. Comprehensive cover is optional but recommended for valuable cars.

Which cars are cheapest to maintain in Nigeria?
Generally popular Toyota and Honda models, because parts are widely available and mechanics know them well.

title: How to Inspect a Used Car Before You Pay: A Complete Checklist
excerpt: A thorough inspection can save you millions. Use this complete checklist to evaluate any used car's body, engine, interior and paperwork before you hand over money.
content:
Never buy a used car without inspecting it

A careful pre-purchase inspection is your best defence against expensive surprises. Whether you do it yourself or hire a professional, work through this checklist before paying for any used car in Nigeria.

Exterior and body

  • Check panel gaps - uneven gaps suggest accident repair.
  • Look for paint mismatches or overspray that hint at a respray.
  • Inspect for rust, dents and cracked lights.
  • Check that the tyres match and have even, adequate tread.

Engine bay

  • Look for oil or coolant leaks.
  • Check the oil level and colour - milky oil is a serious warning.
  • Start the engine cold and listen for knocks, rattles or smoke.
  • Confirm there are no dashboard warning lights after start-up.

Interior

  • Test every electric window, the air-conditioning, lights and wipers.
  • Check the infotainment, reverse camera and all seat adjustments.
  • Assess wear on the seats, pedals and steering wheel against the claimed mileage.
  • Smell for damp, which can indicate past flooding.

Test drive

  • Confirm the transmission shifts smoothly with no jerks or slipping.
  • Listen for suspension knocks over bumps.
  • Check the brakes stop the car straight without vibration.
  • Make sure the steering is straight and does not pull to one side.

Paperwork and identity

  • Verify the VIN matches across the dashboard, door jamb and documents.
  • Run a VIN history check for accidents, title status and odometer records.
  • Confirm customs and ownership papers are complete and genuine.

Trust, but verify

If anything on this checklist raises doubt and the seller cannot explain it, walk away. Buying from a dealer who already inspects, verifies and discloses condition removes much of this risk. Every vehicle on the Korrect Cars inventory passes a multi-point inspection before listing.

Tools to bring to an inspection

You do not need a full workshop to inspect a car, but a few simple items make a big difference:

  • A torchlight to look under the car, inside wheel arches and around the engine.
  • A small magnet wrapped in cloth: if it doesn't stick to a steel panel, there may be thick body filler hiding repair work.
  • Paper towels or a clean rag to check the colour of engine oil and transmission fluid.
  • An OBD-II scanner (inexpensive and widely available) to read stored fault codes, even ones that have been cleared recently.
  • A friend to watch for smoke from the exhaust when you start the engine and to check lights while you press the pedals.

Signs of flood damage

Flooded cars are a serious problem in Nigeria and abroad, and many end up being sold on. Water damage can cause electrical faults that appear months later. Look and smell carefully:

  • A musty or damp smell, or a strong air freshener trying to hide one.
  • Rust on seat rails, seat-belt buckles, screws under the dashboard or the spare-wheel well.
  • Mud, sand or water lines inside the boot, under the carpets or behind the door panels.
  • Foggy headlamps or condensation inside the instrument cluster.
  • Electrical gremlins: windows, locks or dashboard lights that behave strangely.

Red flags that should end the deal

Some problems are not worth negotiating over. Walk away if you find:

  • A VIN that doesn't match on the dashboard, door pillar and papers.
  • Blue or thick white smoke from the exhaust once the engine is warm.
  • Milky residue under the oil cap, which can point to a head gasket problem.
  • Jerky or slipping gear changes in an automatic.
  • A seller who refuses an independent inspection or pushes you to pay immediately.

Should you pay for a professional inspection?

For most buyers, yes. A trained mechanic with diagnostic equipment can spot problems that are almost impossible for a non-expert to find, from hidden accident repairs to failing transmissions. The cost of an inspection is tiny compared with the cost of one major repair. If a dealer offers its own inspection report, read it carefully, and you are still entitled to bring your own mechanic.

After you buy: the first week

Even after a good inspection, plan a basic service soon after purchase: change the engine oil and filters, check the brakes and tyres, and top up all fluids. This gives you a clean starting point and a record of the car's condition when you bought it. Start the change of ownership process promptly so the car's papers are in your name.

Frequently asked questions

How long should a test drive be?
At least 20–30 minutes, long enough for the engine to reach full temperature, and on a mix of smooth and rough roads.

Can I inspect a car at night?
Avoid it. Daylight shows paint differences, dents and leaks much better.

What if the seller says the car was just serviced?
Ask for receipts or service records, and still check the oil and fluids yourself.

Should I check the spare tyre and tools?
Yes. Make sure the spare, jack and wheel spanner are present and in good condition. They are easy to forget and annoying to replace.

title: Why Buying From an Online Car Dealership in Nigeria Is Safer Than You Think
excerpt: Online car dealerships are changing how Nigerians buy cars - with more transparency, verified listings and doorstep delivery. Here's why it can be safer than the roadside market.
content:
The old way of buying cars is changing

For years, buying a car in Nigeria meant trekking around dusty car marts, negotiating with sellers you'd never see again, and hoping the car was as good as it looked. A trustworthy online car dealership flips that model - and done right, it is safer and more transparent than the traditional market.

Transparency you can verify

A good online dealer publishes real photos of the actual car, the verifiable VIN, honest condition disclosures and a clear Naira price. You can research the vehicle before you ever pick up the phone. That openness is hard to get from an anonymous roadside seller who benefits from you knowing less.

Accountability after the sale

An established online dealership has a name, a reputation and a customer base to protect. That gives them every reason to treat you fairly and remain reachable after the sale - unlike a one-off seller who disappears once the money changes hands.

Inspection and verification built in

Reputable online dealers inspect vehicles before listing and stand behind their descriptions. You are buying from someone who has already done part of your due diligence, not from a stranger hoping you won't look too closely.

Convenience and choice

You can browse dozens of verified cars from your phone, compare prices instantly, and filter by make, model, budget and body type - then arrange inspection or doorstep delivery. It saves days of driving around and dramatically widens your choice.

How to buy online safely

  • Choose a dealer with real photos and verifiable VINs.
  • Confirm the price is transparent and all-in.
  • Arrange an inspection or independent check before final payment.
  • Only pay into official, verifiable accounts.

The future of car buying

Online dealerships bring transparency, accountability and convenience to a market that badly needed all three. Korrect Cars was built on exactly these principles - verified vehicles, honest pricing, and support before and after the sale. Browse the inventory to see the difference.

Common scams in roadside and informal car sales

Most car sellers in Nigeria are honest, but the informal market has well-known traps. Knowing them is the best protection:

  • Cloned or stolen vehicles: a car with a copied VIN or plate number, sold with fake papers. The buyer often loses both the car and the money when it is recovered.
  • Rolled-back odometers: a high-mileage car made to look nearly new.
  • Hidden accident or flood damage: fresh paint and new carpets covering serious structural or electrical problems.
  • "Deposit to hold" tricks: sellers who ask for money upfront for a car you have not seen in person.
  • Fake documents: forged proof of ownership, vehicle licence or customs papers.

A reputable online dealership reduces these risks because its business depends on its reputation. One bad sale shared on social media can cost a dealer far more than the profit on a single car.

What a good online dealer should give you

Not every website that sells cars is a trustworthy dealership. Before you buy, look for these signs:

  • A real, verifiable address and phone numbers that are answered by people, not just a WhatsApp link.
  • Clear, recent photos of the actual car from several angles, including the interior and engine bay.
  • The VIN shown or shared on request so you can check it yourself.
  • Honest descriptions that mention faults and wear, not just "accident-free, first body" on every car.
  • Willingness to let you or your mechanic inspect and test drive the car before payment.
  • A written receipt and a proper handover of all documents.

Paying safely

Payment is where many buyers get burned. Pay into a company account in the dealer's business name, not a personal account belonging to someone you have never met. Avoid paying cash in a car park. Get a written receipt that lists the car's VIN, make, model and price. If you are paying in instalments or through a financing partner, read the agreement carefully and keep copies of everything.

After the sale

A good dealer does not disappear once the money clears. Ask what support you get after the sale: help with changing ownership, recommendations for trusted mechanics, and a clear way to reach someone if something goes wrong in the first few weeks. This is where buying from an established online dealership really pays off compared with a one-off private sale.

The bottom line

Buying a car online is safest when you combine a reputable dealer with your own checks. Verify, inspect, then pay.

Frequently asked questions

Can I see the car before paying?
You should always be able to inspect and test drive a car before paying in full. Be wary of anyone who refuses.

Is it safe to pay a deposit online?
Only to a verified business account, with a written agreement that explains when the deposit is refundable.

What documents should I receive?
Proof of ownership, vehicle licence, customs papers for imported cars, a receipt, and any service records available.

title: Top 5 Fuel-Efficient Cars for Lagos Traffic
excerpt: Lagos traffic punishes thirsty engines. These five fuel-efficient cars will keep your fuel spend down while staying reliable and comfortable.
content:
Why fuel efficiency matters in Lagos

Nothing drains a fuel tank like Lagos gridlock. Stop-start crawling burns fuel while you barely move, so choosing a fuel-efficient car can save you real money every single month. Here are five smart choices that balance economy with reliability and comfort.

1. Toyota Corolla

The Corolla is the benchmark for economical, dependable motoring in Nigeria. Its efficient four-cylinder engine sips fuel, parts are everywhere, and it holds its value. For pure running-cost sense, it is hard to beat.

2. Honda Accord

The Accord offers a bigger, more comfortable cabin than most economy cars while remaining reasonably efficient. Its engines are smooth and reliable, making it a great choice for those who want space without a heavy fuel bill.

3. Toyota Camry

A mid-size sedan that manages impressive economy for its size. The Camry's efficient engines and smooth transmission make it comfortable in traffic and easy on fuel, with the bonus of excellent resale value.

4. Hyundai Elantra / Sonata

Modern Hyundai sedans pair efficient engines with generous equipment and a comfortable ride. They offer strong value, keeping both purchase price and fuel costs in check.

5. Toyota RAV4

If you need an SUV but worry about fuel, the RAV4 is the answer. It is far more economical than large body-on-frame SUVs while still giving you ground clearance and practicality for rough roads.

Tips to stretch every litre

  • Keep tyres properly inflated.
  • Service the engine and replace air filters on time.
  • Avoid aggressive acceleration in traffic.
  • Don't carry unnecessary weight.

Spend less at the pump

The right car plus good habits can cut your monthly fuel spend significantly. Browse economical, reliable models on the Korrect Cars inventory and drive smarter through Lagos traffic.

What really makes a car fuel-efficient in traffic

Official fuel economy figures are measured in controlled tests, not in Lagos rush hour. In real stop-start traffic, three things matter most. First, engine size: a smaller four-cylinder engine burns far less fuel idling than a V6. Second, weight: lighter cars need less energy to get moving again every few metres. Third, the gearbox: modern automatics and CVTs keep the engine at low revs, which saves fuel when you are constantly creeping forward. That is why compact sedans and small SUVs with 1.8 to 2.5-litre engines tend to be the cheapest to run in heavy traffic.

What about hybrids?

Hybrids such as the Toyota Prius, Camry Hybrid, Corolla Hybrid and RAV4 Hybrid are built for exactly the kind of driving Lagos produces. At low speeds they can creep along on electric power, and they recover energy every time you brake. The savings in traffic can be significant.

Before you buy one, think about two things. The hybrid battery is expensive to replace, so check its health with a proper diagnostic scan and ask about its age. And make sure there is a mechanic near you who understands hybrid systems. If both boxes are ticked, a hybrid can be one of the smartest buys for a heavy city driver.

Fuel-saving habits that cost nothing

  • Keep tyres properly inflated. Under-inflated tyres increase rolling resistance and fuel use, and they wear out faster.
  • Drive smoothly. Gentle acceleration and early braking save more fuel than any gadget.
  • Don't idle for long periods. If you will be parked for several minutes, switch off the engine where it is safe to do so.
  • Use the AC wisely. Air-conditioning does use fuel, but at higher speeds driving with windows down creates drag that can cost even more. Keep the AC well serviced so it cools efficiently.
  • Remove extra weight. Heavy items left in the boot every day add up over time.
  • Plan your trips. Combining errands and avoiding the worst traffic hours is the biggest saving of all.

Maintenance that keeps fuel use down

A poorly maintained engine can use noticeably more fuel than a healthy one. Change engine oil and filters on schedule, replace a dirty air filter (Lagos dust clogs them quickly), check spark plugs at the intervals in the owner's manual, and fix any warning lights promptly. A faulty oxygen sensor, for example, can quietly increase fuel consumption for months before anyone notices.

Choosing for your own route

Think about where you drive most. A short daily trip in heavy traffic favours a small engine or a hybrid; regular highway journeys make a larger, more comfortable car more sensible. Matching the car to your real driving pattern saves more fuel than any single feature.

Frequently asked questions

Which is more economical in traffic, a sedan or an SUV?
Generally a sedan, because it is lighter and more aerodynamic. Compact SUVs like the RAV4 are close behind and offer extra ground clearance.

Are bigger engines always worse on fuel?
In stop-start city driving, almost always. On open highways the gap is smaller.

Do fuel additives help?
Regular servicing and good-quality fuel make a much bigger difference than additives.

title: Mercedes-Benz GLE 63 AMG: Is the Super-SUV Worth It in Nigeria?
excerpt: 603 horsepower, handbuilt V8 power and genuine luxury - but is the Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 the right super-SUV for Nigeria? Here's an honest look.
content:
The GLE 63: a super-SUV with a handbuilt heart

The Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 sits at the summit of the GLE range - a luxury SUV with the soul of a sports car. Powered by a handbuilt 4.0-litre V8 biturbo making around 603 horsepower, it launches to 100 km/h in under four seconds while carrying five people in diamond-quilted comfort. But does a super-SUV make sense in Nigeria? Let's be honest about it.

What makes it special

Beyond the monstrous engine, the GLE 63 gets AMG's Performance 4MATIC+ all-wheel drive, adjustable air suspension, a quad exhaust, huge brakes, and a cabin dripping with technology - dual widescreens, premium audio, a head-up display and every driver aid Mercedes offers. It is genuinely fast and genuinely luxurious.

The case for buying one

  • Presence: Few vehicles command a room - or a road - like an AMG GLE 63.
  • Performance: The V8 delivers effortless, addictive power.
  • Comfort: It is a true luxury SUV, not a stripped-out sports car.
  • Exclusivity: It signals success without saying a word.

The realities to consider

  • Fuel: A 603-horsepower V8 is thirsty, especially in traffic. Budget accordingly.
  • Maintenance: AMG servicing and parts cost more than standard models. Use a specialist.
  • Premium fuel: The engine wants high-octane fuel to stay healthy.

Who should buy it

The GLE 63 is for the buyer who wants the very best - a fast, luxurious, statement SUV and has the budget to run it properly. If you can absorb the fuel and maintenance, few vehicles deliver this blend of speed, luxury and presence.

The verdict

For the right owner, the Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 is absolutely worth it - a super-SUV that thrills and pampers in equal measure. Just buy a well-verified example and maintain it properly. See premium Mercedes-Benz models on the Korrect Cars inventory.

Living with a GLE 63 day to day in Lagos

On paper the GLE 63 is a track weapon. In reality, most of its life in Nigeria will be spent crawling through Third Mainland Bridge traffic, nosing over speed bumps in Lekki estates and squeezing into tight parking at Ikeja malls. The good news is that it handles that life better than you might expect. In Comfort mode the air suspension softens noticeably, the gearbox shifts early and quietly, and the cabin is calm enough for long calls. The bad news is that a heavy, powerful V8 SUV will always be thirsty in stop-start traffic, and the low-profile tyres that look so good on the 21- or 22-inch wheels are vulnerable to potholes and sharp kerbs.

If you buy one, plan your routes a little. Avoid flooded roads in the rainy season, use the raised ride height setting on rough estate roads, and budget for at least one spare set of premium tyres a year if you drive it often.

Running costs to expect

Owning a super-SUV is less about the purchase price and more about what it costs to keep it perfect. Before you commit, talk honestly with yourself about these areas:

  • Fuel: The V8 is designed for performance, not economy. Expect noticeably higher fuel bills than a GLE 350 or a Toyota Highlander, especially in traffic.
  • Tyres and brakes: Large performance tyres and big AMG brake discs cost several times more than those of a regular SUV, and they wear faster if you enjoy the power.
  • Servicing: Use a workshop with genuine Mercedes diagnostic equipment and AMG experience. Cheap servicing on a car like this usually becomes expensive repairs later.
  • Insurance: Comprehensive cover is strongly recommended, and premiums reflect the car's value and theft risk.
  • Parts: Some AMG-specific parts may need to be ordered from abroad, so factor in waiting time as well as cost.

Buying a used GLE 63: what to check

A well-kept GLE 63 is a joy. A neglected one can be a money pit. Before paying, insist on:

  • A full VIN check to confirm the exact model, year, mileage history and whether the car has been in a major accident or flood.
  • A computer diagnostic scan for stored fault codes, especially for the engine, transmission and air suspension.
  • Air suspension test: the car should sit level after standing overnight, and raise and lower smoothly.
  • Service records showing regular oil changes with the correct grade of oil. Turbocharged V8s are sensitive to neglect.
  • A test drive long enough to get the engine fully warm, listening for rattles, whines or rough gear changes.

Alternatives worth considering

If you love the idea of the GLE 63 but want lower running costs, the GLE 350 or GLE 450 gives you much of the same comfort and presence for far less. If you want speed with more practicality, a well-specified BMW X5 or Porsche Cayenne is worth a look. And if reliability matters more than anything, a Lexus RX 350 or Toyota Land Cruiser will rarely let you down on Nigerian roads.

Frequently asked questions

Is the GLE 63 good for Nigerian roads?
It copes well thanks to adjustable air suspension, but large wheels and low-profile tyres need care on potholed roads.

Can any mechanic service it?
It is best serviced by a workshop with Mercedes diagnostic tools and AMG experience. General mechanics may miss problems specific to the V8 and suspension.

Is a used GLE 63 a good investment?
Like most luxury performance cars, it loses value faster than mainstream SUVs. Buy it because you will enjoy it, not as an investment.
